Name: -1_did_evaluators_job_dream
Representative_Docs: ["My thoughts haven't changed at all since yesterday. As for my speech itself, I thought I did reasonably well in describing my dream job, except perhaps a bit of rambling towards the end.", 'Since leaving the lab I have reflected some in my speech performance. I haven’t exactly been dwelling on what I could have done better but rather I have been focused on the sensory and emotional experience of going through such a simulation. The exercise made me think about real life scenarios and job prep. The high stakes situation of talking about an ideal job made the simulation more nerve wracking. It wasn’t just like doing any random interview for just any job. The evaluators being in a group was interesting and looking back it was clear I focused most on the guy on the left and kind of barely looked at the others.  I also randomly was intrigued by the experience bc this was the second time in my life using vr so I was also thinking about the novelty of that. I thought about the visual aspects of the evaluators specifically race, gender and age. I wondered how my experience would have been different had they been different in appearance. They were all white men with glasses which felt weird and random to me. After learning they’re European professors it made sense contextually but upon first encountering them I really wondered why the evaluators were represented as such.', 'I recall my heart beating out of my chest during the 3 minute preparation section but that the beating became quiet when the evaluators re-entered the room. I felt I could share a convincing narrative of my dream job even with internal doubts I did not plan to share, nor did I share them, with the evaluators. The middle evaluator was calm and neutral, besides some smiles along the way. The left and right evaluators gave polar opposite signals and seemed to swap the signals at one point in the session. I don’t believe these signals impacted my performance though they did shift my attention momentarily if there was a strong movement like a nod or head shake. I felt more conscious that I talked with my hand or looked to the ceiling, the first of which was discouraged. I felt somewhat calmer after the task was completed, and I had some nervous laughter at the very end when removing the sternum tape because it tickled and hurt, though perhaps that opened me to be more expressive about the awkwardness of the evaluation. I felt mostly ok about this in the moment and after, both immediately and in the following day, because the weight of the evaluators’ evaluation is less consequential. I wonder how I might respond in a panel of future managers of mine at a dream company/position. I certainly do get nervous when presenting for my PhD.']

I have also thought back to the moment the evaluators first came into the room. I laughed a little out of both nervousness and surprise. I think this could've been caused by the nervousness I was feeling as a result of the disinterested body language and lack of eye contact from the evaluators.", 'To be honest, I was no longer role-playing as an interviewee after I left the research building. The first time I saw them in person, they seemed a bit threatening. By the second time they came in for the speech, my assumptions about how they would react to me or my presentation had shifted entirely.
For example, the left evaluator seemed very attentive and interested. Name: 13_ability_guy_men_instead
Representative_Docs:
["I knew that the speech task wouldn't have any real consequences regardless of how well or badly I performed, but I still think it was embarrassing. I thought about how the reviewers probably had to fill out a form after assessing my nervousness and body language, and that makes me more embarrassed because I don't want them to think about me or the speech again. I know I did bad, but I hope I didn't do so bad that they think about me beyond their assessment of my performance (if they were tasked with evaluating me). I also disliked the prompt a lot and wish it would have been different. I know that I am not qualified for my dream job yet, so that just made selling myself for the position hard. I think it's especially hard to talk about that stuff at a place like Yale where everyone is doing amazing and you relatively are not. I didn't like talking about jobs and things like that even in regular conversation when I was undergrad here at Yale because it really amped up my impostor syndrome, so everything was just intensified in this situation. I also still wish my interviewers were women, I would have felt much safer. Men scare me and white men do especially. Or even if the interviewers were still all men, I would have been more comfortable with a woman still in the room.", "I thought it was a fun experience overall. Being told to try to keep my hands still prior to the start of the speech gave me a bit of anxiety because it's hard to focus on not using my hands while talking. Other than that, I thought it was fine. I can ramble. Could I have been more eloquent in my delivery? Certainly. Though why try to be perfect when that's an impossible task? The expectation of being liked and perceived well by everyone is anxiety inducing in itself. If others do not like me or judge me negatively, it's normal. I dislike some people and I judge others. Everyone does. It's pointless to worry about each impression one makes. Some people will like you, and that should be enough. I remember laughing after the evaluators left. Focusing on being still while attached to wires did give me slight anxiety. I could tell the middle guy was relatively neutral. The left guy and right guy basically swapped their mannerisms. Left was disengaged at first, yet he was engaged at the end. Right did the opposite. In the end, it doesn't matter what they thought of me.", "Mostly I keep cringing and yearning for death (I don't mean seriously) about how I came across on the study
But the questions seem to presuppose the problem was with my ability or self-concept; I didn't then and don't now feel stupid for what I said (or my inability to say it); I have always been awkward, and the setup of the task (so on the nose to make one self-conscious) I felt actually ended up relieving the worry. And I don't feel stupid for how I speak; speaking is one of the ways I can stave off feeling horrible. 
Instead, the study made me cringe endlessly, pains me now, because it connected up with preexisting problems with self-concept that I am hateable, pretentious, arrogant, etc., and also socially incompetent 
In many ways I wish I would have come across as more conventionally self-conscious, with awkward body language, because then I would at least meet with pity. Instead, I feel like I came across so strangely and arrogantly, and idiotically began to talk about the psychodynamics of graduate school or academic life, to an audience which could interpret it as insulting. 
So the self-consciousness and awful feelings are high, but they're not related specifically to ability; ability is all I have, and was so outwardly compromised by circumstances. Instead, self-consciousness manifested by latching onto preexisting agonies about the impossibility of being received right socially....
And everyone in the study was close in age to me too, both the evaluators and the person I interacted with who administered the study to me...."]
